The third article: whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual knowledge.

Regarding the third point, we proceed as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual knowledge. First, because those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known according to us. But universals are prior according to nature, because that from which the sequence of being does not return <note>original: "a quo non conuertitur subsistendi consequentia"</note> is prior; therefore, universals are posterior in the knowledge of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior as far as we are concerned than simple things. But universals are simpler; therefore, they are known later by us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the Physics that the thing defined comes into our knowledge before the parts of the definition. But more universal things are the parts of the definition of less universal things—just as "animal" is part of the definition of "man"—therefore, universals are known later by us. Furthermore, we arrive at causes and principles through effects. But universals are certain principles. Therefore, universals are known later by us. On the contrary is what is said in the first book of the Physics: that it is necessary to proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the knowledge of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual knowledge in some way takes its beginning from sensitive knowledge. And because the sense is of singulars while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the knowledge of singulars is prior for us than the knowledge of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potentiality to act. Everything that proceeds from potentiality to act reaches an incomplete act—which is midway between potentiality and act—before reaching a perfect act. Now, the perfect act to which the intellect reaches is complete knowledge, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; however, the incomplete act is imperfect knowledge, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known in a certain respect in act and in a certain way in potentiality. Whence the Philosopher says in the first book of the Physics that "things which are first manifest and certain to us are rather confused. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly." 

It is manifest, moreover, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both a universal whole (in which parts are contained in potentiality) and an integral whole can be known; for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in a universal whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing; just as knowing "animal" indistinctly is to know animal insofar as it is an animal. To know animal distinctly, however, is to know animal insofar as it is rational or irrational, which is to know a man or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect to know "animal" before knowing "man." And the same reasoning holds if we compare any more universal thing to a less universal thing. And because the sense goes out from potentiality to act just as the intellect does, the same order 

<column-break/>

of knowledge appears in the sense. For according to sense, we judge the more common before the less common, both according to place and according to time. According to place, as when something is seen from a distance, it is first grasped as being a body before it is grasped as being an animal; and it is first grasped as being an animal before it is grasped as being a man; and first as a man before as Socrates or Plato. According to time, however, because a child from the beginning first distinguishes a man from a non-man before he distinguishes this man from another man. And therefore children, from the beginning, call all men "fathers," and later they determine each one, as is said in the first book of the Physics. And the reason for this is manifest: because he who knows something indistinctly is still in potentiality to know the principle of distinction, just as he who knows the genus is in potentiality to know the difference. And thus it is clear that indistinct knowledge is midway between potentiality and act. 

It must therefore be said that the knowledge of singulars is prior for us than the knowledge of universals, just as sensitive knowledge is prior to intellectual knowledge. But both according to sense and according to intellect, knowledge of the more common is prior to knowledge of the less common. 

To the first, therefore, it must be said that the universal can be considered in two ways. In one way, according as the universal nature is considered together with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality—namely, that one and the same thing has a relation to many—proceeds from the abstraction of the intellect, it is necessary that, according to this mode, the universal is posterior. Whence in the first book On the Soul <note>Aristotle, De Anima</note> it is said that "the universal animal is either nothing or it is posterior." But according to Plato, who posited subsistent universals, according to this consideration the universal would be prior, because particulars according to him do not exist except through participation in the subsistent universals which are called Ideas. 

In another way, it can be considered with respect to the nature itself, namely of "animality" or "humanity," as it is found in particulars. And thus it must be said that the order of nature is twofold. One is according to the way of generation and time, according to which way those things that are imperfect and in potentiality are prior. And in this way, the more common is prior according to nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For an animal is generated before a man, as is said in the book On the Generation of Animals. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior according to nature than potentiality, and the perfect prior to the imperfect; and by this mode the less common is prior according to nature than the more common, such as man is prior to animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of an animal but intends to generate a man. 

To the second, it must be said that the more common universal is compared to the less common both as a whole and as a part. As a whole, indeed, insofar as in the more universal, there is contained in potentiality not only the less universal but also others; as under "animal" not only man but also horse is contained. As a part, however, insofar as the less common contains in its definition <note>original: "ratione"</note> not only the more common but also others, as "man" contains not only "animal" but also "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our knowledge than "man." But "man" is prior in our knowledge than the fact that "animal" is a part of his definition. 

To the third, it must be said that any part can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing prevents knowing the parts before the whole, as stones before a house. In another way, according as they are parts of this whole, and thus it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we first know the house with a certain confused knowledge before we distinguish its individual parts. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defining terms considered absolutely are known before the thing defined; otherwise the thing defined would not be made known through them. <summary>Thomas Aquinas discusses whether universal concepts are known before specific ones, concluding that while we perceive singular things first, our intellectual understanding proceeds from general, confused concepts to specific, distinct ones.</summary>
